entities.summary:
Septimius was a Roman usurper of the later third century CE who briefly proclaimed himself emperor amid the Crisis of the Third Century, when military revolts and short-lived breakaway regimes fractured imperial authority. Like many ephemeral claimants, he is known chiefly through terse notices that record his bid for power and rapid suppression.

The crisis rewarded frontier armies that could elevate commanders, then punished those who failed to hold Italy or key mints. Septimius’s revolt fits the pattern of provincial usurpation: local military support, a grab for imperial titles, and collapse when loyalist forces or rival pretenders prevailed.

Such minor usurpers matter less as personalities than as symptoms—evidence that the mid-imperial system of succession by acclamation had become chronically unstable before Diocletian’s reforms.
